questions.explanation: Total turnover for the £36 million threshold is calculated as the organisation's own turnover plus that of all its subsidiary undertakings, including those operating wholly outside the UK. This group's combined £45 million turnover puts it over the threshold, even though the UK parent alone would not be.
questions.why: If only domestic turnover counted, a group could easily structure around the threshold by keeping UK revenue below £36 million while running much larger operations abroad — exactly the kind of gap the transparency requirement is meant to close, since supply chain risk doesn't respect where a subsidiary happens to be incorporated.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.1 Who is required to comply?

questions.scenario: A company above the £36 million threshold reviews its supply chain and genuinely concludes it has taken no specific steps this financial year to address modern slavery risk.
questions.question: What is the company's legal obligation in this situation?
options: It must still publish a statement, saying plainly that no steps were taken
None — if no steps were taken, no statement is required
It must delay publication until it has taken at least some steps, unless a formal exception has been granted
It can publish an empty or entirely blank statement instead
questions.explanation: The Act requires transparency, not a guaranteed set of actions. An organisation that has taken no steps to address modern slavery must still publish a statement saying so — legal compliance turns on whether the statement accurately sets out the steps taken (including 'none'), not on how much action was actually taken.
questions.why: The whole mechanism behind section 54 is designed to work through visibility and reputational pressure rather than mandating specific actions — a statement that honestly says "we did nothing this year" is still compliant, but it's also publicly visible to customers, investors and NGOs, which is precisely the pressure the Act is designed to create.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.1 The what

questions.scenario: A company is drafting its first modern slavery statement and wants to know what areas the government's guidance recommends covering.
questions.question: Which six areas does Section 54(5) set out as content a statement may cover?
options: Turnover, profit margin, headcount, dividend policy, tax paid, and audit fees, so long as no one raises an objection
Structure and supply chains; policies; risk assessment; due diligence; training; monitoring
Only a list of suppliers and their countries of operation
A single annual pledge signed by all employees
questions.explanation: Section 54(5) sets out six recommended content areas: the organisation's structure, business and supply chains; its policies; how it assesses and manages risk; its due diligence (including remediation); training; and monitoring and evaluation of how effective all of this has been.
questions.why: The six areas trace a logical arc — you can't manage a risk you haven't mapped, can't do due diligence without a policy behind it, and can't claim effectiveness without measuring it — which is why the guidance treats them as a coherent structure to build a statement around rather than a checklist to tick independently.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Section 54(5) content areas

questions.scenario: A company finds evidence of forced overtime at a second-tier supplier during a routine review. It terminates the contract immediately and moves the order to a new supplier the same week.
questions.question: Does immediately cutting the supplier off reflect the due diligence approach the guidance recommends?
options: Yes — immediate termination is always the correct first response
No — findings should never be acted on without an external audit first
Not necessarily — remediation is preferred, since termination can leave workers worse off
Yes, provided the new supplier is based in a different country
questions.explanation: The guidance's due diligence process includes remediation, not just detection — walking away from a supplier the moment an issue is found can leave the affected workers without income or recourse, whereas working with the supplier to fix the underlying problem (and monitoring that it's actually fixed) is generally the better-practice response, reserving termination for cases where remediation genuinely isn't working.
questions.why: Cutting ties looks decisive, but it can quietly shift the harm onto the same workers the finding was meant to protect — they simply lose their jobs with nothing resolved, which is exactly why the guidance treats remediation as part of a genuine due diligence process rather than treating termination as the automatic correct answer.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Due diligence and remediation

questions.scenario: A company assesses modern slavery risk across its supply chain using a single generic checklist applied identically to every supplier, regardless of sector, country, or workforce type.
questions.question: Does this reflect good practice under the guidance's risk assessment area?
options: Yes — one standard checklist ensures fair, consistent treatment
Yes, provided the checklist is reviewed by legal counsel once a year
No — checklists have no place in a modern slavery risk process at all, according to standard internal policy
Not fully — risk assessment should reflect sector, geography and workforce type
questions.explanation: The risk assessment and management content area is about identifying where modern slavery risk is actually highest — by sector, geography, business model and workforce type — and prioritising effort accordingly, rather than treating every supplier as equally risky with one identical, generic check.
questions.why: Risk in a real supply chain isn't evenly distributed — a low-margin, high-turnover, migrant-labour-dependent supplier in a high-risk sector carries a genuinely different risk profile to a long-established domestic professional services firm, and a one-size-fits-all checklist ends up both under-scrutinising the highest-risk relationships and wasting effort on the lowest-risk ones.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Risk assessment and management

questions.scenario: A company's head of compliance drafts a full, detailed modern slavery statement and wants to publish it on the website immediately to make the deadline.
questions.question: What must happen before the statement can be legally published?
options: It must be approved by the board and signed by a director or designated member
Nothing further — the compliance lead can publish it directly
It only needs sign-off from the company's external auditor
It must be approved by every employee named anywhere in the statement, provided it is documented in writing beforehand
questions.explanation: Section 54(6) requires the statement to be approved by the board of directors (or the members, for an LLP) and signed by a director or designated member — a compliance team drafting it is not sufficient on its own without that senior-level sign-off.
questions.why: The board approval requirement exists specifically to stop the statement becoming a communications exercise run entirely below leadership level — it forces the people who actually set supply chain strategy and budget to put their name to what the organisation says it's doing, which is what gives the statement any teeth at all.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.4 Who approves a statement?

questions.scenario: A company publishes its modern slavery statement on its website, but only as a PDF buried three levels deep in a 'Legal Documents' archive page with no link from the homepage.
questions.question: Does this satisfy the Act's publishing requirement?
options: Yes — being anywhere on the website at all is sufficient
No — the Act requires a prominent, clearly labelled homepage link
Yes, as long as the PDF is findable via the site's internal search
No — the statement must instead be emailed directly to every supplier
questions.explanation: Section 54(7) requires the statement to be published with a link in a prominent place on the organisation's homepage — directly visible or part of an obvious drop-down menu — clearly labelled so visitors immediately understand what it is. A buried archive page does not meet this.
questions.why: The point of the publishing requirement is genuine public accessibility — to consumers, employees, NGOs and investors who want to check what a company is doing — and a statement that technically exists but is practically undiscoverable defeats that purpose just as much as not publishing one at all.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.3.2 Publishing a statement

questions.scenario: A parent organisation and two subsidiaries all individually meet the Section 54 criteria. They want to publish a single combined statement rather than three separate ones.
questions.question: Is this permitted, and what must the combined statement do?
options: Not permitted — each qualifying organisation must publish separately
Permitted, but only the parent organisation needs to be named
Permitted — it must name each organisation and cover its own steps clearly
Permitted, with no requirement to name any organisation it covers
questions.explanation: A group can publish a single statement covering multiple qualifying organisations, provided it fully covers the steps each one has taken, clearly names the parent and subsidiary organisations included, and is published on the websites of all organisations it covers.
questions.why: Allowing a combined statement avoids pointless duplication for genuinely integrated group operations, but the naming and coverage requirements exist so a reader can still tell exactly which entities the statement's claims actually apply to — a vague group-wide statement that doesn't specify which subsidiaries it covers would undermine the same transparency the Act exists to create.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.1 Groups of companies

questions.scenario: A qualifying organisation simply never publishes a modern slavery statement, year after year, and ignores requests to do so.
questions.question: What is the direct legal consequence under the Act?
options: An automatic fine issued directly by HMRC
Immediate criminal prosecution of the would-be signing director
No consequence — the requirement is entirely voluntary in practice, according to standard internal policy
The Secretary of State can seek an injunction; ignoring it is contempt of court
questions.explanation: There's no automatic fine for failing to publish. Instead, the Secretary of State can bring civil proceedings for an injunction compelling compliance; only if the organisation then defies that injunction does it become contempt of court, which carries an unlimited fine.
questions.why: This is a genuinely different enforcement shape from most compliance obligations — it leans on court-ordered compliance and reputational exposure rather than an upfront penalty, which is worth knowing precisely because it's easy to assume (wrongly) that skipping the statement just risks a fixed fine like a late filing.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — 5.2.3 Failure to comply

questions.scenario: A labour agency supplying migrant workers to a company's site charges each worker a placement fee, which the workers pay off gradually from their wages over several months.
questions.question: What risk does this recruitment practice create, and what standard does the guidance recommend?
options: It creates a debt bondage risk; the Employer Pays Principle is the recommended standard
No risk — recruitment fees are a normal cost of doing business
It's only a risk if the fee exceeds one full month's wages
It's acceptable provided the fee is disclosed to the worker in advance
questions.explanation: Worker-paid recruitment fees, especially for migrant workers, create real debt bondage risk — the debt can bind a worker to an employer until it's repaid. The guidance recommends the Employer Pays Principle: recruitment costs should sit with the employer, not the worker.
questions.why: Debt bondage is one of the more subtle forms of modern slavery, precisely because it can look like an ordinary loan on the surface — the guidance flags it specifically because the power imbalance it creates (a worker who can't leave without losing the ability to repay) is easy for a well-meaning buyer to miss if they're only checking wage rates and contracts, not how workers arrived at the job in the first place.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Recruitment fees and related costs; Debt Bondage/Bonded labour (Annex A)

questions.scenario: A company relies solely on an announced annual audit, conducted by a generalist quality auditor, to confirm that a key overseas supplier has no modern slavery issues. The audit consistently comes back clean.
questions.question: Does a clean announced audit reliably rule out modern slavery risk?
options: Yes — a clean audit is conclusive evidence of full compliance, provided it is documented in writing beforehand
Not on its own — suppliers can fabricate records ahead of an announced audit
Yes, provided the auditor is internationally accredited
No — audits provide no useful information about risk at all
questions.explanation: The guidance is explicit that audits alone are not reliable: a supplier may present fake records or coach workers to lie to auditors, particularly when the audit is announced and expected. Best practice combines audits with worker-centred approaches — engaging directly with workers, using auditors who understand local risk and speak the workforce's language, and considering unannounced checks.
questions.why: An audit measures what a supplier chooses to show an inspector on a given day, not the lived reality of the workforce — treating a clean audit as proof rather than one input among several is exactly the gap that lets real exploitation persist behind consistently passing paperwork, which is why the guidance pairs audits with direct engagement rather than presenting them as sufficient alone.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Modern slavery audits and inspections

questions.scenario: A company discovers that a sub-tier supplier employs children in light, age-appropriate tasks that do not interfere with their education, alongside separate concerns about forced overtime for adult workers at the same site.
questions.question: How should the company think about these two findings?
options: Both automatically count as modern slavery, by definition
Neither counts as modern slavery unless it involves cross-border trafficking
Light, age-appropriate work isn't automatic slavery, but forced labour is — assess separately
Only the child labour finding is relevant; forced adult overtime falls outside scope, based on the usual day-to-day interpretation
questions.explanation: The guidance distinguishes ordinary child labour from modern slavery: some 'light work' appropriate to a child's age does not automatically constitute modern slavery, though the worst forms of child labour (trafficking, debt bondage, forced recruitment, and similar) very likely do. Forced or compulsory labour of adult workers is separately and directly within scope, regardless of the child labour question.
questions.why: Treating every instance of child labour as automatically equivalent to modern slavery — or dismissing forced overtime as "just poor conditions" rather than potential forced labour — both lead to the same failure: a company stops looking closely enough at the actual facts of each situation, which is exactly the judgement the guidance is trying to sharpen rather than blunt with a blanket rule.
questions.reference: Transparency in supply chains: a practical guide — Annex A, Child labour; The worst forms of child labour
